power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_exact.summary_text: We found 1 imprecise *p* value out of 5 detected *p* values.

table.formatted: Mean Jaccard indices using stPRS-CRC versus PGS003852 as anchors, each compared with the same 27 published PRS, were 0.29 versus 0.20, 0.43 versus 0.25, and 0.27 versus 0.19, respectively (all P<0.001).
table.expanded: Mean Jaccard indices using stPRS-CRC versus PGS003852 as anchors, each compared with the same 27 published PRS, were 0.29 versus 0.20, 0.43 versus 0.25, and 0.27 versus 0.19, respectively (all P<0.001).

table.formatted: All statistical tests were two-sided, with P<0.05 considered statistically significant.
table.expanded: All statistical tests were two-sided, with P<0.05 considered statistically significant.

table.formatted: Comparing individuals in the highest 10% of each PRS with the remaining 90%, 27 of the 28 PRS had ORs greater than 1, and 16 were significantly associated with CRC (P< 0.05) (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1a</ref>).
table.expanded: Comparing individuals in the highest 10% of each PRS with the remaining 90%, 27 of the 28 PRS had ORs greater than 1, and 16 were significantly associated with CRC (P< 0.05) (Figure 1a).

table.formatted: Using the same 27 comparator PRS, the mean anchored Jaccard index was 0.29 for stPRS-CRC, compared with 0.20 for PGS003852, P<0.001 (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>).
table.expanded: Using the same 27 comparator PRS, the mean anchored Jaccard index was 0.29 for stPRS-CRC, compared with 0.20 for PGS003852, P<0.001 (Table 2).

table.formatted: Using the same 27 comparator PRS, the mean anchored Jaccard indices for stPRS-CRC were 0.43 and 0.27 in the AoU validation cohort and the GHI, respectively, compared with 0.25 and 0.19 for PGS003852, both P<0.001 (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>).
table.header: Validation of stPRS-CRC in AoU and GHI
table.expanded: Using the same 27 comparator PRS, the mean anchored Jaccard indices for stPRS-CRC were 0.43 and 0.27 in the AoU validation cohort and the GHI, respectively, compared with 0.25 and 0.19 for PGS003852, both P<0.001 (Table 2).

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "P< 0.05", Text = "Comparing individuals in the highest 10% of each PRS with the remaining 90%, 27 of the 28 PRS had ORs greater than 1, and 16 were significantly associated with CRC (P< 0.05) (Figure 1a)."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::
